info.disclaimer: DevLife estimates wellness & arousal signals for productivity insight — it is not a medical device and does not provide diagnosis.
info.stress.title: Stress Level
info.stress.subtitle: Scale 0.0 – 3.0 · derived from HRV
info.stress.what: A live estimate of how much strain your nervous system is under. It rises when your heart-rate variability (HRV) drops below your own normal range — a well-established physiological fingerprint of stress.
info.stress.how:
ratio = current HRV (RMSSD) ÷ your 14-reading baseline

ratio ≥ 0.85  → 0.5   (calm)
ratio < 0.85  → 1.2
ratio < 0.75  → 1.8
ratio < 0.60  → 2.5   (high)

With a live Bluetooth heart rate, an elevated HR raises the score too.
info.stress.science: HRV — the tiny beat-to-beat changes in heart rhythm — is a validated, non-invasive window into the autonomic nervous system. A meta-analysis of 37 studies found psychological stress is reliably linked to reduced HRV, especially vagally-mediated components like RMSSD. We compare against your personal baseline rather than fixed cut-offs because healthy HRV varies widely between individuals.
info.cognitive_load.title: Cognitive Load
info.cognitive_load.subtitle: Index 0 – 100% · mental workload
info.cognitive_load.what: How much mental effort your body is carrying right now — the physiological "cost" of concentration. Sustained high load is when mistakes start to creep in.
info.cognitive_load.how:
cognitiveLoad % = (stress ÷ 3) × 100

Autonomic arousal (the stress index) is used as a proxy for mental workload.
info.cognitive_load.science: Mental workload measurably suppresses HRV: as a task gets harder, time-domain HRV falls in a graded, dose-dependent way. This works because the same prefrontal circuits that sustain focus also regulate the heart (the "neurovisceral integration" model), so cardiac signals track executive demand. HRV is used in the field to gauge operator workload — e.g. surgeons under pressure.
info.autonomic.title: Autonomic Balance
info.autonomic.subtitle: SNS vs PNS · sympathovagal balance
info.autonomic.what: Your autonomic nervous system has two opposing branches. The sympathetic branch (SNS) is "fight-or-flight" — it speeds you up. The parasympathetic branch (PNS) is "rest-and-digest" — it calms you down. The bars show which one is winning right now.
info.autonomic.how:
PNS bar = min(HRV ÷ 80ms, 1)     ← vagal / recovery tone
SNS bar = min(stress ÷ 3, 1)       ← arousal / activation

SNS clearly > PNS → "Fight-or-flight dominant"
PNS clearly > SNS → "Rest-and-digest dominant"
else              → "Balanced"
info.autonomic.science: RMSSD-based HRV is a recognised marker of parasympathetic (vagal) activity, so higher HRV means stronger rest-and-digest tone. Stress shifts this balance toward sympathetic dominance and away from vagal control. The brain and heart continuously negotiate this balance via the brain–heart axis.
info.state.title: Cognitive State
info.state.subtitle: 5 states · Yerkes–Dodson inverted-U
info.state.what: DevLife sorts each moment into one of five states — RELAXED, DEEP_FOCUS, WIRED, STRESSED, FATIGUED — using the inverted-U law: performance peaks at moderate arousal and falls off when you are under-aroused (tired, bored) or over-aroused (stressed, wired).
info.state.how:
Inputs: WHOOP recovery, day strain, the HRV stress index, and live HR if paired.

low recovery / poor sleep       → FATIGUED
high stress / very high strain  → STRESSED
high strain + low recovery      → WIRED
moderate-arousal "sweet spot"   → DEEP_FOCUS
otherwise                       → RELAXED
info.state.science: The Yerkes–Dodson law (1908) — peak performance at intermediate arousal — has been re-validated with modern neuroscience. A cortical disinhibitory circuit was shown to produce peak performance at mid-level arousal, and norepinephrine-driven arousal produces inverted-U brain-network dynamics. Because lower HRV maps to weaker prefrontal control, the high-arousal states are when error rates climb.
info.cqi.title: Code Quality Index (CQI)
info.cqi.subtitle: Index 0 – 100% · "fitness to ship"
info.cqi.what: A single readout of how well-suited your current physiology is for high-quality coding — blending how recovered, how calm, and how regulated you are.
info.cqi.science: CQI is DevLife's own composite — not a clinical score — but each ingredient is independently validated: recovery/sleep readiness, vagally-mediated HRV as a marker of self-regulation capacity, and the HRV-based stress index. The rationale is the neurovisceral link: better autonomic regulation supports the prefrontal control that careful programming depends on.
info.recovery.title: Recovery
info.recovery.subtitle: 0 – 100% · WHOOP daily readiness
info.recovery.what: How ready your body is to perform today, scored each morning by WHOOP from your overnight physiology. Higher = better recovered.
info.recovery.how:
Reported directly by WHOOP (recovery_score) — primarily driven by your
overnight HRV, resting heart rate, sleep and respiratory rate.
info.recovery.science: Recovery readiness is built on the same autonomic markers as the rest of the dashboard: overnight vagally-mediated HRV and resting heart rate. Higher HRV / lower resting HR indicate stronger parasympathetic recovery.
info.hrv.title: HRV (heart-rate variability)
info.hrv.subtitle: RMSSD, milliseconds · WHOOP
info.hrv.what: The tiny beat-to-beat variation in your heart rhythm. Counter-intuitively, MORE variability is healthier — it signals a flexible, well-recovered nervous system. It is the raw signal most of this dashboard is built on.
info.hrv.how:
Reported by WHOOP as hrv_rmssd_milli (RMSSD, in ms). DevLife keeps a rolling
14-reading baseline and reads stress from how far current HRV sits below it.
info.hrv.science: RMSSD is the standard short-term, time-domain HRV metric and reflects parasympathetic (vagal) activity. Reduced HRV is reliably linked to stress and to weaker prefrontal/executive control.
info.strain.title: Day Strain
info.strain.subtitle: 0 – 21 · cardiovascular load
info.strain.what: How much cardiovascular load you have accumulated today, on WHOOP's 0–21 scale. It rises with exertion and elevated heart rate over the day.
info.strain.how:
Reported directly by WHOOP (cycle strain), a logarithmic 0–21 scale derived
from time spent in heart-rate zones across the day.
info.strain.science: Strain summarises cardiovascular exertion; combined with recovery it drives the inverted-U state model — high strain on low recovery pushes you toward the over-aroused WIRED/STRESSED states where error rates rise.

notes.title: Notes -- Planning Board
notes.default_content:
# DevLife -- Sprint Planning

## Today
- [x] Backend WebSocket server
- [x] Ghost brain (Claude integration)
- [ ] Isometric room rendering
- [ ] WHOOP biometric integration

## Ideas
- Ghost should react to **real** stress levels
- Add *coffee machine* easter egg
- Procedural town generation

## Notes
The ghost watches your biometrics and intervenes when
you're stressed or fatigued. Press TAB to see what it sees.

demo.intro_2: What if a game could adapt to YOU?
demo.intro_3: What if it could read your heartbeat...
demo.chapter_desc_2: Flow state. The code writes itself.
demo.chapter_desc_4: The body speaks. Will you listen?
demo.chapter_desc_5: Wired on caffeine. Running on fumes.
